step1_summary: Chief complaint: Recurrent, “weird” neurological episodes over 1.5–2 months.

Current symptoms (episodic): • Pins-and-needles + numbness confined to right hand • Subjective weakness of right arm and right leg; colleague notes abnormal gait • Difficulty holding coffee cup; transient sense of ‘something in throat’ (mild dysphagia) • General fatigue, intermittent nausea • Episodes initially once / week → now a few times per day; each lasts ~3-4 days then resolves.
No symptoms between episodes; none at time of call.
Aggravating/alleviating factors: none identified; spontaneous onset and resolution.
Past medical history: none significant (possible asthma mentioned by doctor but not confirmed by patient).
Family history: Father had carotid endarterectomy for stroke prevention.
Social history: 32-year-old right-handed male plastic-surgery doctor; lives with wife; non-smoker; no alcohol or drug history mentioned.
Vital signs / physical exam: Remote consult – no vitals; no focal exam possible; no deficits while speaking with GP.
Previous labs: Recent GP screen showed normal BP, cholesterol, and diabetes labs.
Imaging: None to date; TIA clinic referral planned.

V: Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA) / Recurrent embolic events: unilateral motor-sensory episodes resolving, positive family history of carotid disease.
Focal cerebral arteriovenous malformation or cavernoma with intermittent ischemia/bleeding: could cause repeated focal deficits.
Carotid artery dissection: young patient with recurrent same-sided events.
I: Multiple Sclerosis (demyelinating, autoimmune-inflammatory): relapsing unilateral sensory+motor deficits lasting days, typical age group.
Post-viral transverse myelitis/encephalomyelitis: episodic limb weakness and paresthesias.
N: Low-grade brain or spinal cord tumour (e.g., oligodendroglioma) causing intermittent focal symptoms from transient edema.
Meningioma near motor cortex causing position-dependent venous congestion and episodic deficits.
D: Cervical spondylotic myeloradiculopathy: intermittent hand paresthesias, limb weakness, gait change.
Vitamin B12 deficiency neuropathy / myelopathy: sensory changes, limb weakness, gait disturbance.
I2: Medication effect/interaction (e.g., aspirin-related intracranial micro-bleeds causing focal deficits).
Toxic neuropathy from unreported substance use.
C: Congenital Chiari malformation with transient cord/brain-stem compression.
Patent foramen ovale with paradoxical emboli causing TIAs.
A: Myasthenia Gravis: fluctuating weakness, dysphagia, worse with activity.
Systemic autoimmune vasculitis (e.g., CNS vasculitis) causing recurrent focal ischemia.
T: Remote minor cervical spine trauma with intermittent nerve-root impingement.
Repetitive-strain carpal tunnel causing hand paresthesias (doesn’t explain leg).
E: Hypoglycemic episodes causing transient neuro deficits and fatigue.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Typical age group; relapsing focal neurological deficits lasting days then improving; both sensory and motor involvement in different body regions; progressive increase in relapse frequency matches MS disease behaviour.
supporting_evidence: Episodes last several days with partial/complete recovery
Combination of sensory (paresthesias) and motor (weakness, gait change) deficits affecting separate limbs
New bulbar symptom (throat sensation) emerging in later episode
opposing_evidence: Deficits appear strictly right-sided (MS often multi-focal and not confined to one hemisphere)
No optic neuritis, diplopia, or visual loss reported
Episode frequency (multiple per day) is faster than classic MS relapses

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Recurrent Transient Ischemic Attacks (large-artery or cardio-embolic)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Unilateral deficits with complete resolution, positive family history of carotid atheroma; GP suspicion significant, although duration >24 h is atypical.
supporting_evidence: Purely unilateral symptoms (hand, arm, leg, bulbar) suggest vascular territory
Complete return to baseline between episodes
Family history of significant carotid disease
opposing_evidence: Patient is young with normal BP, cholesterol, glucose, non-smoker
Episodes reportedly last 3–4 days (exceed TIA limit of 24 h)
Frequency now several per day without crescendo nature of typical carotid TIAs

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Hemiplegic / Complex Migraine (migraine aura without headache)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Can cause transient unilateral sensory and motor deficits plus nausea; some patients lack significant headache.
opposing_evidence: Duration (days) far exceeds typical migraine aura hours
Presence of objective limb weakness with days-long course uncommon

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Cervical Spinal Cord / Nerve-root Compression (e.g., cervical disc or spondylosis)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Can explain hand paresthesias, arm weakness, gait change via myelopathy; episodic nature could correlate with posture/inflammation.
supporting_evidence: Hand paresthesias and arm weakness on same side
Gait disturbance indicates possible cord involvement
opposing_evidence: Leg and throat symptoms less typical for isolated cervical radiculopathy
Episodes spontaneously remit for days, not classic for structural compression
Young age makes degenerative spondylosis less likely
